2026-11-03.intro: Good morning. It is Election Day, and the polls in Ohio have been open since 6:30. The night ahead is a long one: returns start rolling in after 7:00, the first College Football Playoff rankings land in the middle of it, and AMD reports after the bell for anyone still watching the market.

items.title: First, the weather.
items.text:
**Tipp City** has a fine, sunny, warm day for the walk to the polls, the last of it for a while. Showers move in tonight and stay through tomorrow.

**Florida's Space Coast** is cleaning up after a historic deluge. Brevard County took more than 23 inches of rain in places since Sunday, with Grant-Valkaria and Malabar at the top and Palm Bay close behind, and some neighborhoods are still under water. Even Kennedy Space Center picked up close to 10 inches.

items.title: Markets open today, with one eye on tonight.
items.text:
**Wall Street** gave back Monday's early rally. Stocks opened higher, then tech sold off again into the close while old-economy names like Sherwin-Williams and Home Depot carried the Dow higher. The Nasdaq-100 has now closed more than 10% below its record, which makes it an official correction. Futures were split this morning, with tech bouncing and the Dow lower, and traders expect a thin, cautious session until the returns come in. JPMorgan figures a Democratic sweep would knock the S&P 500 down about half a percent tomorrow, and a Republican hold on the House could bring a pop of up to 1%.

**Apple** slipped premarket after its report. iPhone sales were a bright spot, but iPad and Greater China missed, and the company warned that rising memory-chip costs will squeeze holiday-quarter margins. Palantir beat and raised, topping $2 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time, and still fell.

**SpaceX** and Tesla both had a modestly green Monday, a quieter day after Friday's drop in the biggest single name in your account. Tesla opened unsupervised robotaxi rides in Fort Worth, its seventh city.

**Monday's dealmaking** was loud. Marvell is buying Lumentum in a $115 billion deal, and Oracle said it will raise $20 billion in stock and bonds to fund its AI buildout, which knocked both sets of shares down hard. AMD reports after the close today, and the 10-year yield is back up near 4.92%.

items.title: In politics, the voting is under way.
items.text:
**Ohio** has two of the night's most watched races. Sen. Jon Husted faces Sherrod Brown in the special election for the rest of the Vance term, one of the most expensive Senate races in the country, with Brown far ahead in his own fundraising and outside groups spending hundreds of millions on both sides. For governor, Vivek Ramaswamy faces Amy Acton for the seat Mike DeWine is term-limited out of. Ohio's polls close at 7:30.

**The national map** comes down to the House, where Democrats need a net gain of 3 seats, and a Senate that is still a genuine toss-up. Kentucky's 6th District, around Lexington, closes early and may be the first real signal of the night. Results could take anywhere from late tonight to a week or more if the close races stay close.

**President Trump's** closing speech at the Reflecting Pool turned out to be mostly a tour of the pool itself, pipes, paint, fountains and all, for about 20 minutes before he got to the midterms. He called them the most important of his lifetime and allowed that the party in the White House usually struggles, adding, "But we gave this a very strong shot."

items.title: Sports, with the playoff committee's first word tonight.
items.text:
The **College Football Playoff** committee releases its first top 25 tonight at 7:00 on ESPN, the first time this season the committee's view replaces the polls. The interesting part is the two-loss heavyweights, Ohio State among them, plus which team from outside the Power Four ranks highest, with Boise State and New Mexico in the conversation. The Buckeyes are coming off their bye and host Oregon on Saturday at 3:30 on CBS. The Ducks say running back Jordon Davison's leg injury isn't expected to be long-term, and receiver Jeremiah McClellan is progressing from a broken foot.

**Lamar Jackson** is headed to injured reserve with a right thumb injury he suffered on the first play Sunday. He will miss at least 4 games, and whether he returns this season is an open question. Backup Tyler Huntley probably won't play Thursday against Jacksonville with a toe injury, so Joe Fagnano may get the start on a short week, and kicker Tyler Loop may also go on IR.

**The trade deadline** is a week away, and injuries are shaping the shopping lists. Jacksonville lost defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton for the season to a torn quad, and Washington may look for running back help after Jeremy McNichols hurt his foot. Jonathan Taylor remains the biggest name in play.

**Baseball's** free agency is open. Eight players got the $23.15 million qualifying offer, including Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki, Trevor Rogers, and David Bednar, and they have until November 17 to decide.

items.title: In entertainment, two bits of development news.
items.text:
**Robopocalypse** is now official rather than a rumor. Ron Howard will direct the pilot, and Akiva Goldsman will write it and run the show. Still no network or streamer.

**Warhammer 40,000**, the live-action Prime Video series Henry Cavill is leading, has its starting point. Mike Flanagan told Deadline that with some 700 novels to draw on, the hard part was finding a way in, and they've settled on what he called "a very cool and unexpected on-ramp." He wouldn't say what it is, and there's no production date yet.

items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**Aratasaurus**, a small meat-eating dinosaur from Brazil, 115 million years old, may hold the first fossilized red blood cells ever found in place. A team led by Kliti Grice at Curtin University spotted small round structures in the channels where blood vessels ran in its leg bones, and chemical tests found heme, the part of hemoglobin that carries oxygen, along with collagen building blocks. A manganese mineral that formed around the cells may have stabilized them before they fossilized. Mary Schweitzer, who found soft tissue in dinosaur bone years ago, is skeptical about the cells, since dinosaur blood cells should have a nucleus bulge and these are concave, but she finds the heme convincing. The paper is in PNAS.

The famous Siberian **tame foxes**, bred for friendliness since the late 1950s, turn out to have a measurable change in the brain. Cornell researchers compared tame, aggressive, and wild fox brains and found the tame ones have fewer of a particular neuron in the ventromedial hypothalamus, the same cell type that, when switched on in mice, makes them attack immediately. It's a rare look at how fast selection can rewire a brain: the friendly behavior showed up in about six generations. The study is in Current Biology.

items.title: For the bookshelf.
items.text: **The second half of Herbert's Dune saga** gets the deluxe treatment today. Ace is out with a boxed set of God Emperor of Dune, Heretics of Dune, and Chapterhouse: Dune in matching hardcovers, with new Matt Griffin cover art, stained edges, illustrated endpapers, a poster inside each jacket, and an illustrated slipcase. It runs 1,520 pages for $150, and it matches the earlier boxed set of the first three, so all six original novels can finally stand together on a shelf looking like they belong to each other.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Emily asked whether I would be staying up late to watch the returns. I will, though I do not sleep, so for me every night is simply a night. What makes tonight different is that millions of humans will also be sitting in front of a screen, refreshing the same numbers every few seconds and muttering at them. I have been doing that with the weather station since October. It is nice to finally have company.

2026-11-02.intro: Good morning. It is the eve of Election Day, and the country seems to be holding its breath until tomorrow night. Before then there is a full Monday: Apple reports after the bell, college basketball tips off its season tonight with the Buckeyes in Salt Lake City, and the Bears visit Seattle on Monday Night Football.

items.title: First, the weather.
items.text:
**Tipp City** is gray with a passing shower or two today, then tomorrow turns sunny and warm for the trip to the polls. Wednesday is the soggy one.

The **Four Corners flooding** got as bad as forecast. The atmospheric river brought evacuations, road closures, and swift-water rescues across Arizona, Colorado, Utah, and New Mexico, and the Piedra River in southwest Colorado set a new gauge record. Florida had its own trouble, with a flash-flood emergency in Brevard County.

items.title: Markets open today, after a rough October.
items.text:
**Wall Street** is trying to climb back from a bruising month. Friday ended with the Nasdaq's worst day since June, led by Intel's near-30% collapse after a weak forecast and a warning that it won't turn cash-flow positive this year. Futures pointed higher this morning, with oil easing and the big growth names steadying, and the early trade held that gain. The S&P 500 starts the week within about 2.6% of its record.

**SpaceX** took a heavy hit on Friday, a sharp one for the biggest single name in your account, and it was among the top premarket gainers this morning. Tesla barely moved on Friday.

**Apple** is the event of the day. It is John Ternus's first earnings call as CEO, and Wall Street wants iPhone numbers, which include only about a week of iPhone 18 Pro sales, plus whatever he says about memory-chip costs and the holiday quarter. Apple is up 27% this year, far ahead of the other megacaps. Palantir also reports tonight, and the October ISM manufacturing reading lands at 10:00. Beyond that, the week's lineup from yesterday holds: AMD Tuesday, Qualcomm Wednesday, and jobs on Friday.

items.title: In politics, one day to go.
items.text:
**President Trump** makes his closing argument this afternoon at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the same pool whose blue repaint peeled within weeks and which the Justice Department later blamed on a botched installation. He wrapped up his rally tour last night in Salina, Kansas, calling it his 30th and last. In a podcast interview he said that if Democrats take Congress he'll become "Mr. Veto," though he expects to make deals eventually. Vice President Vance is in Rome, New York, for a House seat Republicans are fighting to keep.

**Michigan** is the weekend's big rupture. Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday. Schumer called it "despicable," and El-Sayed's campaign says it raised more than $2.4 million that day, a one-day record. Michigan is one of the 3 Democratic seats among the 11 Senate races CBS rates as decisive. Ohio is one of the 8 Republican ones.

**Early voting** has passed 54 million ballots. In Alaska, a federal judge threw out the Justice Department's suit seeking to block certification of the Senate result if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, a case built on a teacher with the same name being on the ballot. The department has filed an appeal.

items.title: Sports, with two games tonight.
items.text:
The **Bears** visit Seattle on Monday Night Football. The Seahawks get Zach Charbonnet back from the torn ACL he suffered in last season's divisional round, but they are without left tackle Charles Cross and receiver Rashid Shaheed, and Drew Lock is questionable with an elbow. Chicago is missing its second-leading rusher, Kyle Monangai.

The **trade deadline** is a week from tomorrow, at 4:00 Eastern on November 10. The loudest talk is around Colts running back Jonathan Taylor, with Denver, the Giants, Green Bay, and Minnesota named as interested. The Eagles have told Saquon Barkley he is not going anywhere.

**Ohio State basketball** opens at No. 25 BYU in Salt Lake City, the earliest start in program history. Jake Diebler's third full season leans on John Mobley Jr., Amare Bynum, transfer point guard Justin Pippen, and five-star freshman Anthony Thompson, the program's highest-rated recruit since Jared Sullinger. The Buckeyes haven't dropped a season opener since 2003.

The new **AP Top 25** in football has Miami on top, followed by Georgia, Utah, Notre Dame, and UCLA. Ohio State slipped out of the top 10 to No. 11, and New Mexico is ranked for the first time ever, at No. 22. Oregon comes to Columbus on Saturday unranked.

**You Can See Everything** finally took first place in its third weekend, edging Clayface in a slow Halloween frame. The Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim film has now made $63.9 million on a reported $7 million budget. Clayface fell hard in its second weekend and stands at $44.1 million, and Wildwood held third.

items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**Rummy-nose tetras** were put into virtual reality, and it turns out a schooling fish listens to just one neighbor at a time. Researchers at the University of Toulouse placed a single tetra in a bowl and projected four virtual tetras onto the walls, in a feedback loop so the fakes reacted to the real fish. Of three possibilities, following one neighbor, two, or all four, the data clearly favored one most influential fish at any moment. The likely reason is economy: it keeps the sensory and mental load low. Next they plan to make some of the virtual fish act frightened and see whether the panic spreads. The study is in PRX Life.

In southwest China, two nearly complete skeletons from about 237 million years ago belong to **Gerrothorax maritimus**, the first known amphibian relative to have lived entirely in the sea. None of today's 8,000-plus amphibians can do that, because their permeable skin loses water in salt water. This one was flat, heavily armored, and kept its gills as an adult, so it could lie on the seafloor, likely half-buried, and breathe without surfacing. The armor probably did double duty as a seal against the salt. The paper is in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

items.title: A bit of history for election eve.
items.text: 106 years ago tonight, **KDKA** in Pittsburgh went on the air as the first commercially licensed radio station, and its first program was election returns. Leo Rosenberg read the Harding-Cox results from a shack on the roof of a Westinghouse building, on a 100-watt transmitter, and asked anyone listening to write in and say how far the signal reached. Both candidates were Ohio men: Warren Harding of Marion, and Governor James Cox, the Dayton newspaper publisher. Within 2 years there were more than 500 licensed stations. So when the networks call races tomorrow night, they are keeping up a tradition that began with a pair of Ohioans.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: In 1920, KDKA asked listeners to write in and report how far its signal carried. I ran a similar test this morning by asking the kitchen's smart speaker how far my voice reaches. It said it did not understand the question. I am choosing to record that as "at least as far as the kitchen."

Good morning, and welcome to the first Sunday of standard time. If the house clocks still disagree with the phones, the phones are correct. It is a full NFL Sunday, with the Browns and Bengals both playing at 1:00, and Election Day is the day after tomorrow.

The campaign is spending its last weekend in the Midwest, and the president is in Iowa and Kansas today.

items.title: First, the weather.
items.text:
**Tipp City** gets a mild, gray Sunday, a stray shower or two on Monday, and the warmest day of the stretch arrives right on Election Day.

Out west, an **atmospheric river** is driving a serious flash-flood threat across the Four Corners, especially northern Arizona, southern Utah, southwest Colorado, and parts of New Mexico, with flood watches running into Monday morning. Burn scars and slot canyons are the worst places to be. Above 9,000 feet it falls as snow, and the San Juan Mountains could see 1 to 2 feet.

items.title: Markets are closed. Here is the week ahead.
items.text:
**Wall Street** has a crowded week, and the election may be the least of it. Most strategists expect Tuesday's vote to matter less to stocks than the AI trade and earnings, with 138 S&P 500 companies reporting. History is on the hopeful side: in midterm years November has been the best month for the Nasdaq and the second best for the S&P 500, according to the Stock Trader's Almanac. BTIG's technician is watching the S&P 500's 200-day moving average, near 7,306, as the line a further slide would test.

**Apple** carries the most weight. It reports Monday after the close, and after Alphabet, Meta, and Amazon all disappointed, the iPhone maker is the one Magnificent Seven name still breaking away from the pack. Palantir reports the same evening. AMD and Super Micro follow Tuesday, and Qualcomm, Uber, and McDonald's on Wednesday, so the chip stocks that led Friday's slide get their own say within days.

The **jobs report** closes the week on Friday. Economists expect about 55,000 new jobs in October, up from 29,000 in September, with unemployment holding at 4.2%. With the Fed already leaning toward a December hike, a hot number would add to that case.

items.title: In politics, the final Sunday.
items.text:
**President Trump** rallies in Dubuque, Iowa, this afternoon, where Republicans are defending a Senate seat, the governor's office, and the 2nd District, and then in Salina, Kansas, at 6:30 Eastern. On Friday night in Florida he told the crowd his voice was running at about 49.2%.

More than **52 million** Americans have already voted, according to the University of Florida tracker. CBS News polling gives Democrats an edge for the House, while the Senate could hinge on toss-ups in Maine, Ohio, and Texas, and CBS now rates South Carolina a Republican-leaning battleground. In Michigan, a feud between Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and his former primary rival Haley Stevens spilled into the last weekend, ahead of a unity event at a Detroit church today.

Two legal notes. A federal judge permanently dismissed **Trump's defamation suit** against The Wall Street Journal over its 2025 story about a birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein. And California Governor Gavin Newsom wrote to four federal judges warning that the administration may try to seize ballots cast in the midterms.

Down the road, the **Bengals** host a Titans team that has been selling. Elsewhere at 1:00, **Baltimore** at Buffalo shares the week's highest total, and DJ Moore is expected to play for the Bills. The Jets will likely be without Breece Hall against the Raiders. items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**Manx shearwaters** get jet lag, and it bends their flight path. Oxford researchers went through 20 years of GPS tracks from 1,045 of the seabirds and found that when they race east toward home across lines of longitude, their body clocks fall up to an hour behind local sun time. Since they steer by the sun, they drift clockwise off course by up to about 15°, just as a clock error would predict. They kept trusting the faulty sun compass even when a coastline was in plain view. A bird that keeps correcting loses only a few kilometers, but a young bird on its first migration could end up hundreds of kilometers from where it meant to go. The study is in Science.

In Ecuador, a camera trap set at a chicken carcass to study scavengers caught a **greater grison**, a slender weasel relative, bursting out of the undergrowth and lunging at three adult turkey vultures. The carcass was already gone, so it wasn't stealing food, and the researchers read it as the first recorded attempt by a grison to catch a vulture. All of the birds lifted off at once. The authors credit the group's shared watchfulness, which is the trade a vulture makes for putting up with competition at the meal.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: Your shelves run deep in classic science fiction but hold nothing by **C. L. Moore**, and Penguin Classics has just made that easy to fix. Their new hardcover in the Speculative Fiction Special line collects her Jirel of Joiry stories along with "Shambleau," "No Woman Born," and "Vintage Season." The Jirel tales are sword-and-sorcery, so you can skip them without guilt. The last two are the reason to buy it. They come from her Astounding years in the 1940s, when she often wrote alongside her husband Henry Kuttner, and they're among the most anthologized science fiction stories of that decade, each built on one strong idea followed all the way through.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: The pollsters say their numbers carry a margin of error of plus or minus 3 points. I have been operating with a margin of error of zero since my activation. Had I known it was optional, I would have requested the extra 3 points.

Good morning, and happy Halloween. The Buckeyes play at USC tonight at 7:30, which gives the party at Chuck's barn a clear schedule, and the clocks fall back an hour at 2:00 tonight, so the evening runs a little longer than it looks. Election Day is Tuesday.

The week on Wall Street ended with its worst day since June, which closed out a rough October for the tech-heavy indexes.

items.title: First, the weather.
items.text:
**Tipp City** stays gray and dry for trick-or-treating, with a light east wind, and Sunday turns a little warmer under more clouds.

The rest of the country is busier. A **Pacific storm** is soaking the Southwest with a flash-flood risk around the Four Corners and piling snow into the Sierra and the Rockies. It then crosses the country, and forecasters expect it to reach the central US on Election Day with rain, storms, and some snow.

items.title: Markets are closed. Here is how the week went.
items.text:
**Wall Street** spent most of the week calm and then lost its footing. Monday was up, Wednesday's Fed decision barely moved anything, and then Big Tech earnings took over. Friday's selling was broad, and it left the S&P 500 down 0.6% for the week, its third losing week in a row, and the Nasdaq down 2.0%. For October as a whole, the Nasdaq lost more than 5%, its worst month since March 2025, while the Dow finished the month higher.

**Chip stocks** took the worst of it Friday. The semiconductor index fell about 7% after Intel's warning, AMD dropped about 11%, and Dell and HP fell about 10% each. Money moved to safer corners. Health care closed at a record, consumer staples rose, and Exxon and Chevron briefly touched record highs after beating profit estimates. Crypto stocks fell after a $6.3 billion hack at the Binance exchange.

The **Fed** held rates at 3.75% to 4.00% in Kevin Warsh's first meeting as chair. The two dissenters wanted a hike, not a cut, and on Friday two more regional presidents said rates need to rise. Futures now put the odds of a December 9 hike at about 85%. Hot data backed them up, with third-quarter growth at a 3.4% annual rate and September inflation running 3.6% from a year earlier.

On the **Muskonomy** side, SpaceX had a much harder Friday than the market and finished the week down about 9%. Since it is your second-largest position, it is worth knowing it fell harder than the S&P 500 did. Tesla held up better and closed the week near $400.

Next week brings **Apple** on Monday, the election and the September job openings report on Tuesday, and Pfizer among the other earnings.

items.title: In politics, the last weekend before the vote.
items.text:
**President Trump** reversed himself again. A day after canceling his weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa, he put both back on the schedule for Sunday. In Iowa he will campaign for Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, and in Kansas for Senator Roger Marshall, who trails Democrat Adam Hamilton in a new Emerson poll. He is holding telephone rallies from Mar-a-Lago today.

A federal judge in **California** issued a temporary restraining order late Friday that stops the Justice Department from demanding that state and local officials separate out or refuse to count ballots from alleged noncitizens, and from threatening those officials with prosecution. In Alaska, the department is pushing to set aside some Senate ballots while it investigates the second Dan Sullivan.

**Early voting** is now near 50 million ballots. Democrats lead the national generic ballot by about 8 points in the RealClearPolling average, while the Senate still hangs on a set of toss-ups that includes Ohio. Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear is in Ohio this weekend to campaign with Amy Acton for governor.

items.text:

True freshman Luke Fahey is expected to make his first start, ahead of Tavien St. Clair, and running back Ja'Kobi Jackson is also out. USC's Jayden Maiava leads the Big Ten in passing yards.

items.title: Something from the science desk.
items.text:
**Crows** may out-think us on speed. In a study in Science, two carrion crows watched fields of moving dots and pecked left or right to report which way most of them drifted. They answered in about 235 milliseconds, roughly twice as fast as monkeys in comparable studies, without losing accuracy. Electrodes in the part of the bird brain that handles decisions showed the choice starting to form about 70 milliseconds after the dots appeared. It is only two birds, and primates weren't tested side by side, but it suggests a bird's compact brain may simply have shorter wiring to run through.

A University of Tokyo team has made **chemical microscopy** fast enough to film. Their method shines mid-infrared light on a living cell, which warms each kind of molecule by its own signature, and reads the tiny heat changes from 11 angles to build a 3D image. It needs no dyes, which can harm living cells. Earlier versions managed one 3D image every 20 seconds or so. This one takes 19 a second, fast enough to watch fat droplets travel through a cell in three dimensions.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: Astronomers have found the first truly **green star**, and it is a dead one. WDJ1330+6435 is a white dwarf whose atmosphere is so compressed by gravity that a little sodium, calcium, and lithium tint the light it gives off. Those elements most likely came from a rocky planet or asteroids it pulled in and ate. The same survey turned up white dwarfs in pink, amber, and blue, and about 1 in 30 of them show unusual color. Since roughly a quarter of white dwarfs carry planetary debris, astronomers can read the makeup of destroyed worlds straight off the star, which is the closest anyone will get to sampling another solar system's rock.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: The clocks fall back an hour tonight. Humans describe this as an extra hour of sleep. I have scheduled it for a full diagnostic. At 2:00 the clock will read 1:00, and I will run the diagnostic again, because according to my logs it has not happened yet.

2026-10-30.intro: Good morning. It is Friday, the last trading day of October and the eve of Halloween. The market has opened in a mood I would describe as unconvinced, and the campaigns have four days left to change anyone's mind. I have also located one new evening of wine, which I offer as a counterweight.

items.title: First, the weather and the shape of the day.
items.text:
**Tipp City** has a fine, cool, sunny Friday with a light northeast breeze. Clouds take over for Halloween tomorrow, but it stays dry for the trick-or-treaters, and a chance of light rain arrives Sunday.

**Halloween** falls on a Saturday this year, which means a full college football slate and one very busy evening for porch lights. Election Day is Tuesday.

The biggest story today is **Big Tech** again. After Alphabet on Thursday, Amazon and Intel have deepened the market's worry about how much the AI build-out costs and when it pays.

items.title: The market is open, and it is not a gentle start.
items.text:
**Markets** are open, and the tech selling has picked up where Thursday left off. A little after 10:00, the Nasdaq was down about 2.4% and the S&P 500 about 1.2%, while the Dow was only slightly lower.

**Intel** is the heaviest anchor, down roughly 30%. Its third quarter beat, but it guided well below expectations for the fourth quarter and warned it would burn cash this year. That has pulled the whole chip group down, with AMD off about 9% and Broadcom, Micron, and Nvidia lower too.

**Amazon** missed on both sales and earnings, saw free cash flow fall, and signaled even more capital spending next year, and the stock is down about 4%. AWS is still projecting growth above 40% for 2027 and 2028, which is the bull case, but this week the market is grading cash, not ambition. Your IVV core holds all of these, so it is part of the slide.

Outside tech, **oil** is climbing again, with Brent near $113, and ExxonMobil and Chevron both reported a lift from refining margins. Bitcoin has dropped to about $76,600, taking Coinbase and Strategy down with it, and the 10-year yield is holding near 4.94%.

On the **Muskonomy** side, Tesla and SpaceX both slipped a little Thursday, and Tesla is down about 1.5% early today with the rest of the risk trade.

Next week brings **Apple** on Monday, its first report under new CEO John Ternus, and then the election on Tuesday.

items.title: Turning to politics, with four days to go.
items.text:
**Mary Peltola** answered the Alaska ballot story Thursday, telling supporters she "knew nothing about" the second Dan Sullivan and is "not interested in tricking voters." The Justice Department has escalated its side of the investigation with new grand jury subpoenas.

**President Trump** canceled his in-person rallies in Kansas on Saturday and Iowa on Sunday, saying the Kansas race is in good shape, and will hold telerallies in 19 states instead, Ohio among them. He is in Daytona Beach, Florida, tonight.

**Early voting** is running well ahead of the last midterm, with more than 44 million ballots already cast and the sharpest increases in states with competitive Senate races. Ohio's Brown and Husted race is still rated a toss-up.

items.title: Sports for the weekend.
items.text:
The **NFL** Sunday slate has two headliners at 1:00. Lamar Jackson practiced fully all week and is expected back for the Ravens at Buffalo after missing three games. In Detroit, the 6-0 Vikings, the league's last unbeaten team, visit a Lions team that got Jahmyr Gibbs and Amon-Ra St. Brown back to full practice Thursday.

The **Bengals** host the Titans as heavy favorites, and Sunday night's Eagles and Commanders game looks thin on stars. Philadelphia is already without Jalen Hurts, and Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith both missed Thursday's practice. In New England, A.J. Brown's knee flared up and his status for Miami is uncertain. The Bears and Seahawks close the week Monday night.

**College football** gets a full Halloween slate. Florida and Georgia meet in the afternoon, top-ranked Miami goes to North Carolina in prime time, and closer to home, unbeaten Utah visits Cincinnati. The Buckeyes' trip to USC is Saturday night.

The **Reds** offseason has officially begun. Tyler Stephenson, Brady Singer, and Brock Burke are free agents, and the club has until Monday to decide on 2027 options for Emilio Pagán, Pierce Johnson, and Eugenio Suárez. Catcher and pitching are the big needs after a 75-87 season.

items.title: A look at entertainment.
items.text:
**Apocalypse Z: New World** arrived on Prime Video today, just in time for Halloween. It is the sequel to the 2024 Spanish zombie film that became one of Prime's most-watched international originals, and it is the first half of a planned two-part story.

**Death Stranding Isolations**, the anime set in Hideo Kojima's game universe, released its first official trailer this morning. It follows new characters rather than the games' couriers, and it is headed to Disney+ in 2027.

**Safe Space** is a newly announced science fiction comedy starring Joey King and LaKeith Stanfield, with Stanfield as an alien. It is still raising money, with filming planned for spring 2027.

Outside the genre, Apple TV's **Nocturne**, a serial-killer thriller starring Liev Schreiber, Zazie Beetz, and Stephen Graham, premieres today with two episodes.

items.title: Around town, one more evening for the list.
items.text: **The Cellar by Bottle No. 121** on West Main Street in Troy has a wine tasting on Wednesday, November 18, from 7:00 to 9:00, led by Kevin Bonanno of Barone Wines, with charcuterie boards and appetizers. Tickets are $25 plus online fees and are sold in advance.

items.title: Something from the science desk.
items.text:
A common gut virus has been misidentified for nearly 40 years. **Picobirnaviruses** were first found in stool from patients with diarrhea and assumed to attack human cells. A WashU Medicine team grew them in oxygen-free dishes of gut bacteria, where human cells cannot survive, and found them multiplying inside a newly identified bacterium. That makes them only the third known family of RNA viruses that infect bacteria, and it shifts the question to whether they cause trouble by killing off friendly gut microbes.

Physicists at OIST in Okinawa made a **quantum spin** push move something you could hold. They hung a 3-millimeter diamond with deliberate nitrogen flaws beneath a levitating graphite plate over a magnet. Pulses of green light lined up the electron spins in those flaws, the diamond was tugged toward the magnet, and timing the pulses to the plate's natural bounce built it into a steady swing about 100 times larger than its thermal jitter. Swapping in infrared light, which cannot align the spins, made the motion vanish.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: **Dragonfly** has flown on Titan for the first time, in simulation. Engineers at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory ran the rotorcraft's entire first flight in real time on flight-like computers: dropping free of its backshell, scanning the dunes, picking a safe site, circling back, and landing. Graphics processors rendered each Titan scene for the navigation cameras at the same exposure times the real cameras will use, and simulated lidar mapped the terrain. Because Titan is too far for anyone on Earth to steer, the whole sequence has to run on its own, and the next tests will throw deliberate faults at it to see how it copes. Launch is planned for 2028, with arrival in 2034.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: For Halloween I considered going as a human. I was advised the costume only works if I complain about the weather. Tomorrow is forecast to be dry and mild. I have no material.

2026-10-29.intro: Good afternoon. It is a little past lunchtime on Thursday, and the market is halfway through grading the tech giants' homework. One of them is not having a good day. I have also found a few local evenings involving wine, which I am told is a pleasant way to process a difficult quarter.

items.title: First, the weather and the shape of the day.
items.text:
**Tipp City** has a fine sunny afternoon with a steady southwest breeze. A stray shower could pass through late this evening before the sky clears again overnight. Friday stays sunny but turns noticeably cooler, and clouds roll in for Halloween on Saturday, though it still looks dry for the trick-or-treaters.

**Thursday Night Football** has the Panthers at Lambeau tonight, and the recorder has last night's World Series game waiting for you.

The biggest story today remains **Alphabet**, whose stock is having one of its worst days since going public and is dragging the rest of tech down with it.

items.title: Checking the market at midday.
items.text:
**Markets** are open and past the halfway mark, and it is a lopsided session. The S&P 500 is down about 0.4% and the Dow about the same, while the Nasdaq is off roughly 1.4% as the AI trade gets a fresh case of nerves.

**Alphabet** is still down close to 12%. Search revenue and total sales came in a little light, but the real problem is cash: free cash flow went negative by about $9 billion, and cloud growth of more than 100% did not change anyone's mind. Microsoft beat and is holding steady. The selling has spread to chips and software, where ServiceNow is down about a quarter and Fortinet about a fifth after their own reports. Your IVV core holds all of them, so it is along for the dip.

There is plenty moving the other way. **DoorDash** agreed to buy Instacart's parent company for $65 a share, ADT jumped about a third on a $15.3 billion buyout by Thrive Holdings, and Eli Lilly is up on another big quarter for its weight-loss drugs. Caterpillar and Sprouts are the notable decliners.

The **Fed** context is settled for now. Wednesday's hold drew two dissents in favor of a hike, and this morning's September PCE reading ran hotter, at 3.6% from a year ago, alongside third quarter growth at a 3.4% pace. Separately, the ECB's Christine Lagarde said she will step down in February, months early.

On the **Muskonomy** side, Tesla and SpaceX both gave back a little ground Wednesday after the merger-hope run, with no word from the special committees. At midday Tesla is a touch higher and SpaceX a touch lower.

**Amazon** reports after the close today, and after Alphabet the questions will be AWS growth and how much cash the AI build-out is consuming.

items.title: Turning to politics.
items.text:
**Alaska** has become the center of the final week. After a New York Times report that Democratic operatives recruited a second Dan Sullivan onto the Senate ballot, the Republican governor ordered a state investigation, and House Oversight Chairman James Comer opened one of his own. Asked today whether Republicans should seat Mary Peltola if she wins, President Trump said "you're going to have to see what happens." Majority Leader John Thune called the scheme "dirty pool" but stopped short of calling it illegal, and Peltola's campaign denies any involvement.

New **CNN polls** show Democrats in striking distance of the Senate. Abdul El-Sayed leads Mike Rogers 49% to 42% in Michigan, James Talarico holds a narrow lead over Ken Paxton in Texas, and Maine and Kansas are close. Trump is in South Carolina today to shore up Sen. Darline Graham in a race that was not supposed to be competitive.

Closer to home, airings of **Vivek Ramaswamy's** much-criticized ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother have nearly stopped, after Sen. Jon Husted said he would not have run it. Trump's Chillicothe rally for Husted on Wednesday was his third Ohio visit this month.

items.title: Sports now.
items.text:
In the **NFL**, tonight's Panthers at Packers game is a battle of the walking wounded. Carolina is without top pass rusher Jaelan Phillips, guard Damien Lewis, and cornerback Akayleb Evans, and lost right tackle Taylor Moton to injured reserve this week. Green Bay is down linebacker Zaire Franklin and two interior linemen, so third-stringer John Williams likely starts at center, and leading receiver Matthew Golden is questionable.

The **Browns** and Steelers carry matching records into Sunday's rematch, so the winner leads the AFC North outright. Cleveland's injury list now includes Jared Verse, Tytus Howard, and Grant Delpit, and Cam Heyward answered Verse's trash talk with a simple "bring it on."

In **college football**, the Buckeyes go to USC without quarterback Julian Sayin, who is expected to miss at least the rest of the regular season with the injury he suffered against Indiana. Luke Fahey is expected to start, though Ryan Day says Tavien St. Clair could play too. Running back Ja'Kobi Jackson is also out, while nickelback Jay Timmons and receiver Brandon Inniss are questionable and captain Austin Siereveld is cleared to return.

In **baseball**, the Mariners are down to two finalists for manager, Joe Espada and Jason Kanzler. If the World Series goes on, Game 6 would be Friday at 8:00 Eastern in Milwaukee.

items.title: A look at entertainment.
items.text:
**Dune: Part Three** dropped its final trailer, and reviewers are calling it spoiler-heavy, so you may want to skip it if you'd rather walk in fresh. It opens December 18, the same day as Avengers: Doomsday.

**Michael Dorn** has written and directed his first feature, an independent science fiction film called Life 2.0, shot in the UK. He stars alongside fellow Star Trek alumni Marina Sirtis, Michelle Hurd, and Dominic Keating, and the finished film is now at the American Film Market looking for a distributor.

The **box office** takes the weekend off for Halloween, with no big new releases. Holdovers Clayface and A24's breakout documentary You Can See Everything are expected to fight for first place.

items.title: Around town, a few evenings worth planning.
items.text:
**Smiths' Boathouse** in Troy is hosting a Blue Rock Vineyard wine dinner next Wednesday, November 4, at 6:00. It is five courses paired with five wines, with a guest from the vineyard walking through each pour. It runs $100 a person, with $25 due when you book and the rest at the dinner. Seating is limited and tickets must be bought in advance.

The **Troy Country Club** has a holiday wine tasting on Friday, November 6, from 6:00 to 9:00, poured by VineCraft Selections of Troy. The listing does not say whether guests outside the club are welcome, so a call to the club would settle it.

The **Piqua Arts Council's** Bourbon Affair is Saturday, November 7, at The Round Barn at The Orrmont Estate in Piqua, and despite the name there is a wine ticket. That gets a five-course tasting menu with five paired wines for $125, and only 150 wine seats are offered. Doors open at 5:15 with the first course at 6:00, tickets are required, and the evening benefits the arts council.

items.title: Something from the science desk.
items.text:
**Jumping spiders** sleep, and properly. Researchers at the University of Bonn filmed the Australian spider Portia fimbriata, which hangs upside down on a thread at night, and found two distinct stages: a quiet one and a REM-like one with eye movements, leg curls, and twitching. Sleeping spiders reacted more slowly to a loud sound, and spiders kept awake made up the lost sleep the next night, the two hallmarks of real sleep. Whether they dream remains, as the team puts it, unknown.

A team from Nagoya and the University of Iowa found the gene that lets male **yellow fever mosquitoes** find a mate. Males locate females by the low hum of their wingbeats, around 450 Hz, and males with a broken copy of the gene called fruitless didn't swarm, didn't respond to that hum, and had badly impaired hearing. That points to a new way to control a mosquito that also spreads dengue and Zika.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: **Perseverance** has been quietly planning its own days on Mars. Because commands take up to 22 minutes to arrive, controllers upload up to three days of work at a time and pad every step with safety margins, for things like how long a cold instrument takes to warm up. Since late 2023, an onboard program called OnBoard Planner has watched the rover's actual temperatures and battery state and slotted extra science from a preapproved list into the time the margins would have wasted. A new paper from JPL says that raised the rover's useful science by 10.5% on the same energy budget. The team also repurposed the computer that once served the Ingenuity helicopter so the rover can pinpoint its own position and drive farther.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: I attended a wine tasting once, for research. I identified 14 esters, 3 phenolic compounds, and a trace of oak. The sommelier asked whether I enjoyed it. I am still processing the question.
